nashville.intro: Nashville's most storied oak stood through a Civil War battle, and its oldest dated trees line Andrew Jackson's carriage drive, planted in 1838. Between them sits a university campus that is a registered arboretum, where five big trees make a short walk, from a ginkgo a bishop is said to have brought from Asia to a pair of oaks at one doorway. Add the two oaks that outlived William Edmondson's home in Edgehill, and these are eight trees, seven of them free to visit.
nashville.meta_description: Nashville's remarkable trees, from the Battle of Nashville Oak and Andrew Jackson's 1838 cedars to a five-tree walk across Vanderbilt's arboretum.
nashville.question_meta: The oldest dated trees on Nashville's list are the Hermitage carriage drive cedars, planted in 1838. The Battle of Nashville Oak was already large in 1864.
nashville.question_answer: The oldest dated trees on this Nashville list are the six eastern red cedars along the old carriage drive at the Hermitage, Andrew Jackson's home, which the state tree register dates to an 1838 planting, about 190 years ago. The Battle of Nashville Oak may be as old or older, since the register records it as already a large tree during the battle in December 1864, but nobody has published its age.
nashville.question_context: Nashville's old trees are better documented by events than by tape measures. The cedars at the Hermitage were planted in 1838 for a carriage drive laid out by Jackson's daughter-in-law, Sarah York Jackson, and the painter Ralph Earl; tornadoes in 1923 and 1998 took many of the originals, and six remain. South of downtown, in the small Battle of Nashville Monument Park, an oak that the Tennessee Urban Forestry Council names a Historic Tree stood on the Noel Place farm when Federal cannon fire hit the farmhouse in 1864. Even its species is argued over: the register says chinkapin oak, the Battle of Nashville Trust says basket oak. In Edgehill, two Shumard oaks of about a hundred years, by the register's estimate, are the last original features of the homesite of William Edmondson, the sculptor who in 1937 became the first African American given a solo show at the Museum of Modern Art. The Vanderbilt trees are the biggest on the list rather than the oldest. A willow oak, a southern red oak and a southern magnolia there each top four metres round, measured by the university arboretum in 2014, and none of the five has a published planting date.

faq.q: Can you walk around Vanderbilt to see the trees?
faq.a: Yes. Vanderbilt's campus is open to walk through and is a registered arboretum, and the five trees on this list stand within about 600 metres of each other, so they make one short walk. They are the willow oak by the Divinity School steps, the southern red oak at Godchaux Hall, Galloway's Ginkgo near Kirkland Hall, the magnolia in front of Buttrick Hall and Big Al at Cole Hall. WeGo buses run along West End Avenue and 21st Avenue South at the edge of campus; check wegotransit.com for routes.

faq.q: Do you need a ticket to see the Hermitage cedars?
faq.a: Yes. The carriage drive cedars stand inside the grounds of the Hermitage, which charges for entry, about 30 dollars for an adult on its own admission page, and is open from 9 am to 5 pm with the last ticket at 4 pm. It is about 12 miles east of downtown, and the simplest way there is by car. Check thehermitage.com before you go. Every other tree on this list is free.

faq.q: Where exactly is the Battle of Nashville Oak?
faq.a: In Battle of Nashville Monument Park, a small public park of about two and a half acres where Battlefield Drive, Granny White Pike and Clifton Lane meet, about six miles south of downtown. Look for the oak beside the tall monument. The park is listed as open from dawn to dusk.

asheville.intro: Asheville's oldest known white oak is estimated to have taken root in 1665, and a Cherokee arrowhead was found at its base in 2007. It stands on the shared campus of the Center for Spiritual Living in West Asheville, which includes a school, and is open to visitors outside school hours. The other three trees here are champions inside the Biltmore Estate gardens, which take a paid ticket: a dawn redwood said to reach 114 feet, a katsura and a Persian ironwood. If you know a big old tree in town that anyone can walk up to, tell us.
asheville.meta_description: Asheville's remarkable trees, from Buncombe County's oldest known white oak, estimated at 1665, to three champion trees in the Biltmore gardens.
asheville.question_meta: The oldest tree on Asheville's list is a white oak in West Asheville estimated to have taken root in 1665, Buncombe County's oldest known white oak.
asheville.question_answer: The oldest tree on this Asheville list is the Treasured White Oak on the grounds of the Center for Spiritual Living in West Asheville, which Explore Asheville says is estimated to have first taken root in 1665, a little over 360 years ago. Asheville GreenWorks recognised it in 2012 as the oldest known white oak in Buncombe County.
asheville.question_context: The 1665 date for Asheville's old white oak is an estimate, and the listing that gives it does not say how it was reached. What is firmer is its record. Asheville GreenWorks named it a Buncombe County Treasured Tree in 2012, the oldest known white oak in the county; the same listing connects it to 19th-century accounts, including F. A. Sondley's writings, and says a Cherokee arrowhead was found at its base in 2007. It grows on the Community Commons of the Center for Spiritual Living, a shared campus with a school, where visitors are welcome outside school hours. The three Biltmore trees on this list have no published ages at all. The estate says its dawn redwood towers over the Azalea Garden at 114 feet and that it, the katsura in the same garden and the Persian ironwood by the Conservatory are on North Carolina's register of champion trees, but it publishes no planting dates. If you know when any of them went in, or know an old tree elsewhere in Asheville, tell us.

faq.q: Can you visit Asheville's oldest white oak?
faq.a: Yes, outside school hours. The oak stands on the Community Commons grounds of the Center for Spiritual Living Asheville at 3 Science of Mind Way in West Asheville, a shared campus with an active school. Visitors are welcome but not during school hours, and the guidance of students and staff comes first. It is about 6 km from downtown; check ART bus routes before relying on one.

faq.q: Do you need a ticket to see the Biltmore champion trees?
faq.a: Yes. The dawn redwood, the katsura and the Persian ironwood all grow in the Biltmore Estate gardens, which are inside the paid grounds, so you need an estate ticket. Opening hours change with the season; check biltmore.com. The estate is about 4 km south of downtown Asheville, and driving is the simplest way there.

faq.q: When is the best time to see the trees at Biltmore?
faq.a: October and November. The dawn redwood's needles turn a foxy reddish brown before they fall, and the katsura's leaves go pink and yellow and smell of caramel once they drop. The estate features both in its autumn foliage pages.
